title: Cycles: why property moves in waves, and what that means for timing
summary: Property moves in waves because buildings take years to deliver while demand and credit change in months. Supply, credit, interest rates and cap rates each run on their own clock, and the worst outcomes come when they turn together. You cannot time the top, but you can know where you stand and build a deal that survives the turn.
body:
Mr Shabazz, property moves in waves because buildings take years to deliver while demand and credit change in months. You cannot time the top of a cycle, but you can know roughly where you stand in it and build every deal so that it survives the turn.

Recall

Q. From the law and tax checkpoint, what is the difference between taxing by residence and taxing by source?

A. Residence taxation looks at where the taxpayer lives or is managed and may reach worldwide income. Source taxation looks at where the income arises, such as where a building sits. A cross-border deal can face both, which is why treaties and credits exist.

Q. From using professionals, what should an engagement letter define before any work starts?

A. The scope, who the client is, the deliverables, the fee basis, who may rely on the advice and any limit on liability. If it is not in the letter, assume it is not being done.

Q. From how law works, what is precedent?

A. The principle that courts follow earlier decisions on the same point of law, so that like cases are decided alike. It is the backbone of common law systems and plays a smaller, more persuasive role in civil law systems.

Why this matters

Remi here. Most developers who fail are not bad builders. They are good builders who started the right building at the wrong point in the cycle, or financed it as if the good times would last for the length of the loan. A project takes three to five years from land to stabilisation. Over that span the market you bought into will almost certainly change. The question is not whether the cycle turns during your project, but whether your project can absorb the turn when it comes.

Four clocks that run at different speeds

In plain English, a property market is driven by four things that move on their own timetables. Demand: people and businesses needing space, which follows jobs, incomes and population. Supply: new buildings, which arrive years after the decision to build them. Credit: how easily and cheaply lenders will lend, which can change in a single quarter. And pricing: what investors will pay for a dollar of income, which follows interest rates and sentiment.

The professional framing is the cycle as a sequence. In recovery, vacancy is high but falling and almost nothing is being built. In expansion, rents rise, occupancy tightens and new starts begin. In oversupply, the buildings started during expansion deliver all at once, usually just as demand cools. In recession, vacancy climbs, rents soften and lenders retreat. The heart of the cycle is the supply lag: the gap between the moment a developer decides to build and the moment the building competes for tenants. That lag is the reason markets overshoot. Every developer reads the same strong rents at the same time, starts at the same time and delivers at the same time.

Worked example one, with hypothetical numbers. A city absorbs about 1,000 new apartments a year. Rents rise sharply for two years, so developers file applications for 4,000 units. Construction takes roughly two and a half years from approval. If most of those projects start within the same twelve months, the market receives about four years of demand over a period of two years. Even if demand holds steady, vacancy in new buildings rises and landlords offer free rent to fill them. Nobody made an unreasonable decision on its own. The overshoot came from everyone acting on the same signal with the same delay.

Say that out loud now.

Interest rates, cap rates and the spread

A capitalisation rate, or cap rate, is a property’s net operating income (NOI) divided by its value: the income an investor buys for each dollar paid. When interest rates rise, buyers can earn more on safer investments and borrowing costs more, so they usually demand a higher cap rate, which means they pay less for the same income. The professional framing treats the cap rate as a safe yield plus a risk premium, minus the income growth buyers expect. The difference between a property cap rate and the yield on a long government bond is often called the cap rate spread. The relationship is real but loose and lagged. Cap rates do not move one for one with interest rates, and a wide spread can absorb a rate rise for a while.

Worked example two, hypothetical. A building earns $1,000,000 of NOI. At a 5 percent cap rate it is worth $20,000,000. If cap rates move to 6 percent, the same income is worth $1,000,000 divided by 0.06, about $16,700,000. The building lost about 17 percent of its value without losing a single tenant. If you financed it with a loan of $13,000,000, your equity fell from $7,000,000 to about $3,700,000, nearly half. That is why a one-point move in cap rates feels small in conversation and enormous on a balance sheet.

Timing: position, not prediction

Nobody reliably calls the top or the bottom. What a disciplined developer does instead is read the position. Count the supply pipeline against demand. Watch lender behaviour: loosening terms and rising loan-to-value ratios are late-cycle signs. Watch the spread between cap rates and bond yields: a very thin spread leaves little room for rates to rise. Then design the deal so that it works if you are wrong about timing. That means long enough debt to ride out a downturn, an exit that does not depend on cap rates staying low, and equity that can wait.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is underwriting the peak as if it were normal: today’s record rents and record-low cap rates projected forward for the life of the project. The control is to underwrite with a downside case drawn from the worst year of the last full cycle in that market, and to set your exit cap rate higher than today’s, not equal to it.

The beginner’s mistake

The beginner reads rising rents as permission to build and does not ask who else read the same rents. The professional reads rising rents as a signal that competing supply is about to be approved, and goes to the planning register to count it before buying land.

Six-Lens Check

Tax: a sale in a downturn may produce a loss whose usefulness depends on how and where you hold the asset; verify that against the primary source before you rely on it. Liability: personal guarantees become live exactly when the cycle turns, so know every one you have signed. Banking: lenders tighten together, so a refinance planned for a downturn may not exist; secure term before you need it. Governance: write down who can decide to pause, phase or sell when the market turns, before it turns. Estate: a portfolio built on short debt can force a sale at a low point if you die or become incapable, so your plan should name who holds authority to refinance. Exit: assume you sell at a higher cap rate than you bought; if the deal still works, the cycle is a risk, not a threat.

Callback

In Week 2 you met the outside view and reference classes: before trusting your forecast, ask how similar projects actually performed. A cycle is the outside view stretched across time. The reference class for your exit is not this year’s sales; it is the sales that happened in the weakest year of the last cycle. And in Week 10 you learned that value equals NOI divided by the cap rate, which is the one equation this lesson made move.

Recap

Property cycles exist because supply arrives years after the decision to build, while demand and credit change in months. Cap rates follow interest rates loosely and with a lag, and a one-point move can halve your equity. You cannot predict the turn, so read your position, underwrite the downside and buy time with your debt.

Next: Ford, Failure Forensics — Olympia & York in 1992, a giant built on short money at the top of a cycle.
checklist: Count the full supply pipeline against annual demand before buying land.
Note where lender terms sit compared with the last cycle: loan-to-value, pricing, covenants.
Track the spread between local cap rates and long government bond yields.
Underwrite a downside case from the worst year of the last full cycle.
Set the exit cap rate above today’s cap rate, not equal to it.
Choose debt long enough to ride out a downturn, not just to reach completion.
Write down who can decide to pause, phase or sell, before the market turns.
head: Field checklist
speak: Property moves in waves because buildings take years to deliver while demand and credit change in months. Four clocks run at different speeds: demand, supply, credit and pricing. The supply lag drives the overshoot: everyone sees the same strong rents, starts at the same time and delivers into the same soft market. Pricing follows interest rates loosely. A cap rate is income divided by value, so if a building earns 1 million and cap rates move from 5 to 6 percent, value falls from 20 million to about 16.7 million. With a 13 million loan, my equity nearly halves without losing a tenant. I cannot predict the top, so I read my position instead: the pipeline against demand, how loose lenders are, and how thin the spread over bond yields has become. Then I build every deal to survive being wrong about timing, with long enough debt, a higher exit cap rate and equity that can wait.
terms: Supply lag — the delay between the decision to build and the date the new building competes for tenants or buyers.
Capitalisation rate (cap rate) — a property’s net operating income divided by its value; the yield a buyer pays for.
Cap rate spread — the difference between property cap rates and the yield on long government bonds.

hostile.q: Rents have risen 12 percent in two years. Why are you underwriting them flat?
hostile.a: Because those rents are the signal every other developer is reading. I can show you the applications filed in the last eighteen months against annual demand; if they deliver together, rents soften in my lease-up year. I underwrite flat rents and a higher exit cap, and anything better is upside I have not borrowed against.

role: Failure forensics, with Roman assisting on finance
title: Olympia & York 1992: a giant built on short money at the top of the cycle
summary: Olympia & York became one of the largest office developers in the world, then committed to Canary Wharf in London as the late-1980s boom peaked. When the early-1990s downturn emptied office markets and tenants stayed away, the company could not refinance its short-term borrowing, and in May 1992 it sought creditor protection. The root cause was a long, concentrated bet funded with money that came due inside the cycle.
body:
Mr Shabazz, Olympia & York shows that a world-class developer with a world-class track record can still be destroyed by one decision: putting a very large, long-dated bet on a single market at the top of a cycle, and funding it with money that came due before the bet could pay off.

Recall

Q. From the law and tax checkpoint, what is a flow-through entity?

A. An entity whose income is taxed in the hands of its owners rather than at the entity level, such as many partnerships. The entity files information but the owners report the income.

Q. From using professionals, what is legal professional privilege in concept?

A. Protection that can keep confidential communications between a client and a lawyer, made for legal advice, from being disclosed. It can be lost by sharing the advice widely, and its scope differs by country.

Q. From how law works, why does it matter whether a country follows common law or civil law?

A. It changes where you look for the rules. In common law systems, court decisions build the law case by case; in civil law systems, a written code is the primary source and judges apply it.

Why this matters

Ford here, with Roman assisting on the finance. Olympia & York was not a reckless newcomer. It was a family-controlled Toronto developer that had built landmark office towers and was widely admired for its skill. That is the point of the case. The lesson is not that bad developers fail. It is that good developers fail when the scale and timing of one project outgrow the strength of the balance sheet behind it. This lesson stays with the broad public record; detailed figures varied between accounts, so we avoid them.

Step 1: Timeline

Through the 1970s and 1980s, Olympia & York, controlled by the Reichmann family, built a large portfolio of office buildings, including First Canadian Place in Toronto and the World Financial Center in New York, which proved a success. In the late 1980s it took on Canary Wharf, a vast office development in London’s former docklands, well east of the established financial district. The early 1990s brought a recession and a glut of office space in London. Tenants were slow to commit to a location with weak transport links, and a planned Underground extension that would serve the site had not been built. In May 1992 the parent company sought protection from creditors in Canada, and Canary Wharf was placed into administration in Britain. The extension, the Jubilee line, opened in 1999. Canary Wharf later recovered and became a major financial district under new ownership arrangements.

Step 2: Key decisions

Three decisions mattered. Committing to a project of enormous scale in one market, which tied the fate of the whole group to a single location. Proceeding before the transport link the location depended on was secured. And funding a portfolio of long-lived buildings substantially with borrowing that needed regular renewal, including short-term debt.

Step 3: Assumptions

The core assumption was that London’s financial sector would keep expanding and that tenants would follow quality space to a new district, as they had in New York. The second assumption was that credit would remain available for renewal, because the group’s reputation had always secured it. The third was that the transport problem would be solved in time.

Say that out loud now.

Step 4: Incentives

Banks competed to lend to a famous name, and a strong reputation can substitute for scrutiny. The developer’s own success rewarded boldness: every past bet against conventional wisdom had paid off. Governments wanted the docklands regenerated and welcomed the investment. Few people were paid to say that a single project could sink the whole group.

Step 5: Warning signs ignored

An office supply surge was visible in London as the 1980s boom ended. The transport link was uncertain. Leasing at the new district was slow. And the group’s growing reliance on rolling over debt meant that any tightening of credit would arrive as a liquidity problem, not merely a fall in value. Each sign was public before the crisis.

Step 6: Point of no return

The point of no return was not May 1992. It was the moment the project’s scale and the group’s short-term funding were combined. Once a long, slow-to-lease asset was financed with money that had to be renewed every year or two, the company needed credit markets and tenants to cooperate at the same time. In a downturn, both stopped.

Step 7: Root cause

Roman’s summary: the root cause was a maturity mismatch on a concentrated bet. A long-dated, single-market project was funded with short money, so a cyclical downturn became a refinancing failure. Value fell, as values do in recessions, but it was the inability to renew debt on time that turned a bad market into an insolvency.

The small-developer version

This is a composite example. A developer with three completed buildings starts a fourth that is larger than the first three combined. To fund the equity, she takes a two-year bridge loan secured on the three existing buildings. The new building is late, the market softens, and when the bridge matures the lender will only renew at a lower loan amount. With hypothetical numbers: the bridge is $6,000,000, the lender will renew only $4,000,000, and the $2,000,000 difference must be found in a month when nobody is lending. She sells one of the good buildings at a weak price to pay down the loan. One large bet put the whole portfolio at risk, exactly as at Canary Wharf, at a fraction of the scale.

What a lender should have asked

Roman again. Put yourself in the seat of a bank credit officer around 1989, asked to renew or extend a facility to the group. Four questions would have revealed most of the risk without hindsight. What share of the group’s total equity is committed to this one project? How much of the group’s debt must be renewed in the next 24 months, and what happens if renewal is refused by two lenders at once? What happens to leasing if the transport link slips by five years? And what is the plan if office rents in this market fall by a third, as they had in earlier downturns? None of these questions requires a forecast of the recession. Each tests whether the borrower survives one.

The general lesson is that reputation lowers scrutiny precisely when scrutiny matters most. Lenders and partners relax around a famous name, which allows concentration and short funding to build up unnoticed. When you are the developer, the discipline has to come from you, because nobody else at the table will insist on it while things are going well.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is letting one project grow larger than the balance sheet can carry through a downturn, then funding it with debt that must be renewed during that downturn. The control: cap any single project as a share of your total equity, and match each loan’s term to the date the asset can realistically repay it, tested against the worst year of the last cycle.

The beginner’s mistake

The beginner treats a strong reputation, or a strong relationship with a bank, as if it were committed funding. A relationship is not a facility. Only signed, long-dated debt survives the moment every lender pulls back together.

Callback

In Week 3 you studied overconfidence and the planning fallacy: past success makes people underweight the chance of failure. Olympia & York had more past success than almost any developer of its time, which made the bias stronger, not weaker. And yesterday’s lesson on the supply lag explains the London office glut: projects approved in the late-1980s boom delivered into the early-1990s recession.

Recap

A celebrated developer committed to a giant project in one market at the top of a cycle, before its transport link was secured, funded in part with short-term debt. The downturn turned a fall in value into a refinancing failure. Rule 27 follows from it.

Rule 27: Fund long projects with long money, never let a refinancing date fall where a downturn can reach it unprotected, and never let one project grow larger than the balance sheet can carry through the worst year of the last cycle.

Next: Priya, The Money — how interest rates and cap rates move the size of your loan and the value of your equity.
checklist: Cap any single project as a share of your total equity before you commit.
Match every loan’s term to the date the asset can realistically repay it.
Test each refinancing date against the worst year of the last cycle.
Treat a lender relationship as a relationship, never as committed funding.
Do not proceed until the infrastructure your location depends on is secured or priced.
List every loan that must be renewed in the next 24 months, with its maturity date.
Run the seven steps on any cycle failure you study.
head: Field checklist
rule: Rule 27: Fund long projects with long money, never let a refinancing date fall where a downturn can reach it unprotected, and never let one project grow larger than the balance sheet can carry through the worst year of the last cycle.
speak: Olympia and York, controlled by the Reichmann family, was one of the most admired developers in the world. In the late 1980s it committed to Canary Wharf, a vast office district in east London, at the top of the cycle and before the transport link it needed was built. The early-1990s recession left London with too much office space, tenants were slow to move, and much of the group’s funding needed regular renewal. In May 1992 the parent company sought creditor protection in Canada and Canary Wharf went into administration. The point of no return was earlier: combining a giant single-market bet with short money. The root cause was a maturity mismatch on a concentrated bet. My rule: fund long projects with long money, keep refinancing dates out of a downturn’s reach, and never let one project outgrow what my balance sheet can carry through the worst year of the last cycle.
terms: Maturity mismatch — funding a long-lived asset with debt that falls due before the asset can repay it.
Concentration risk — the danger that one project, market or tenant is large enough to sink the whole portfolio.
Creditor protection — a court-supervised process that pauses creditors’ claims while an insolvent company tries to restructure.

hostile.q: This project is twice the size of anything you have built. What happens to your other buildings if it goes wrong?
hostile.a: Nothing, by design. It sits in its own company with no cross-guarantees, the equity is capped at a fixed share of what we have, and the loan term runs two years past the slow-case stabilisation date. If it fails, it fails alone, and the downside case shows that.

title: How a rate move shrinks your loan and your equity at the same time
summary: When interest rates rise, two things happen to the same building: the lender can lend less against the same income, and buyers pay less for that income. Those effects compound on your equity. Fixed rates, hedges, laddered maturities and lower leverage are how you buy protection, and each has a price.
body:
Mr Shabazz, a rise in interest rates hits a property twice at once. The lender can lend less against the same income, and buyers pay less for that income. Your equity sits underneath both, so it takes the combined blow.

Recall

Q. From this week’s first lesson, what is the supply lag?

A. The delay between deciding to build and the day the building competes for tenants. It is why markets overshoot: many developers react to the same strong rents and deliver together.

Q. From using professionals, how should you challenge advice you doubt?

A. Ask for the reasoning and the assumptions in writing, test them against facts you know, and get a second opinion where the stakes justify it. A good adviser welcomes the question.

Q. From how law works, what is a statute?

A. A law passed by a legislature. Regulations made under it fill in detail, and courts interpret both.

Why this matters

Priya here. Developers often model interest as a single line in the pro forma and forget that the rate also decides how much they can borrow and what the building will sell for. In a cycle, rates change while your project is half built. If you understand the three channels through which a rate move reaches your equity, you can choose which protection to buy and know what it costs.

Channel one: the loan gets smaller

Lenders size loans to the lower of several limits. One of the most important is the debt service coverage ratio (DSCR): net operating income (NOI) divided by the annual loan payments. If the lender requires a coverage of 1.25, the annual payment cannot exceed NOI divided by 1.25. The loan amount that payment supports depends on the rate. Professionals use the loan constant: the annual payment, interest and principal together, as a percentage of the loan. Coverage requirements and constants are commercial practice set deal by deal, not standards; the figures below are hypothetical.

Worked example one. A stabilised building earns NOI of $1,200,000. The lender requires a DSCR of 1.25, so the maximum annual payment is $1,200,000 divided by 1.25, which is $960,000. At a low rate, the loan constant is 6.5 percent, so the maximum loan is $960,000 divided by 0.065, about $14,800,000. Rates rise by two points and the constant becomes 8.0 percent. The maximum loan is now $960,000 divided by 0.08, which is $12,000,000. The building did not change. The loan you can raise against it fell by $2,800,000, about 19 percent.

Say that out loud now.

Channel two: the value falls, and channel three: the cost rises

Higher rates usually push cap rates up, with a lag. Using the same building, at a 5.5 percent cap rate the value is $1,200,000 divided by 0.055, about $21,800,000. At 6.5 percent it is about $18,500,000. That is a fall of $3,300,000.

Worked example two puts the channels together. Suppose you planned to refinance at completion, repaying a $14,000,000 construction loan. In the low-rate world, the new loan of $14,800,000 repays it with a little to spare, and your equity is worth the $21,800,000 value minus the $14,800,000 debt, about $7,000,000. In the high-rate world, the new loan of $12,000,000 leaves a $2,000,000 shortfall you must fund in cash, and your equity is worth $18,500,000 minus the remaining debt. A two-point rate move produced a $2,000,000 cash call and wiped out roughly $3,300,000 of value at the same moment. If any of your debt floats, the third channel adds to it: on a $10,000,000 floating loan, a two-point rise costs about $200,000 a year in extra interest before you even reach the refinance.

Buying protection

There are four main protections, each with a cost. A fixed rate removes the payment risk but usually costs more at the outset and carries a penalty if you repay early. A hedge, such as an interest rate cap, pays you if rates rise above a strike, in exchange for an upfront premium. Laddered maturities spread your refinancing dates so one bad year cannot reach all of them. And lower leverage leaves room for the loan to shrink. The professional move is to price each one against the shortfall in the high-rate case, not against its cost in the base case.

How the best do it

Large institutional owners typically manage refinancing as a portfolio problem rather than a building-by-building one. They spread maturities across years, keep a share of debt fixed or hedged under a written policy, and hold liquidity sized to the next twelve to twenty-four months of maturities. What a small developer can copy is the written policy: one page stating the maximum floating exposure, the minimum remaining term, and the cash held against the next maturity.

Wealth Ledger

Warrick’s note. On your personal balance sheet, equity in a leveraged building is the most rate-sensitive asset you own, because it absorbs the value fall and the loan shrinkage together. Record it at a stressed value, not the broker’s figure. If you have personal guarantees or a personal line of credit secured on property, a rate rise reaches your household directly. Before you add leverage, ask what your net worth would be after a two-point rate rise and a one-point cap rate rise together.

Worked example three: fixed rate or a cap

All figures are hypothetical, and pricing for fixed rates and caps is set by the market at the time; treat these as illustrations, not quotes. You have a $10,000,000 floating-rate construction loan for three years at a floating rate that is today 6 percent. Option A: swap to a fixed rate of 6.5 percent. You pay an extra half point every year whatever happens, $50,000 a year, $150,000 over three years, and you are fully protected. Option B: buy a cap at 7.5 percent for an upfront premium of, say, $120,000. You keep the floating rate while it stays low, and your rate can never go above 7.5 percent.

Now test both against the stressed case, where rates rise two points to 8 percent in year 2 and stay there. Unprotected, years 2 and 3 cost an extra $200,000 a year, $400,000 in total. With the fixed rate, your extra cost over the base was the $150,000 premium, so you saved about $250,000. With the cap, you paid $120,000 and your rate was held at 7.5 percent, half a point above the strike in each of the two bad years, so the cap paid you about $50,000 a year, $100,000 in total, and you still paid 1.5 points above base. The fixed rate wins in this storm; the cap wins if rates stay flat. There is no free answer, only a choice about which future you are paying to survive.

The order of operations

Professionals decide protection in a particular order. First, what the project can survive: the maximum shortfall in the stressed case that committed equity can cover. Second, what remains unprotected after that. Third, which tool covers the remainder most cheaply. Starting with the cheapest tool and working backward to what it covers is how developers end up hedged against the wrong risk.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is planning a refinance on today’s rate and today’s cap rate. The control: size the take-out loan in a high-rate case, hold the shortfall as committed equity or reserve, and decide your hedge policy before the loan closes.

The beginner’s mistake

The beginner shops only for the lowest rate. The professional shops for the structure that survives the cycle: term, extension options, prepayment cost and hedge requirements, and accepts a slightly higher rate to get them.

Callback

In Week 15 you learned that leverage magnifies returns in both directions. Today you saw it from the other side: the same leverage that lifts equity returns when rates fall magnifies the loss when they rise, and it does so through two channels at once. Yesterday’s Olympia & York case was the extreme version, where the refinance simply did not happen.

Recap

A rate rise shrinks the loan the income supports, lowers the value buyers will pay and raises the cost of any floating debt. Combined, they can turn a comfortable refinance into a cash call. Protection exists, and you price it against the stressed case.

Next: REGA, The Rules — the regulations that move with the cycle, and how Canada and Guyana approach them.
checklist: Size the take-out loan at the current rate and at two points higher.
Compute value at today’s cap rate and at one point higher.
Calculate the refinance shortfall in the high-rate case.
List every floating-rate loan and its annual cost per point of rate rise.
Write a one-page debt policy: maximum floating share, minimum term, cash against maturities.
Price fixed rates, caps and lower leverage against the stressed shortfall.
Record leveraged equity at a stressed value on your personal balance sheet.
head: Field checklist
speak: A rate rise hits a building through three channels at once. First, the loan shrinks: the lender limits payments to income divided by the coverage ratio, so on 1.2 million of income at 1.25 coverage the payment is 960,000; that supports about 14.8 million at a 6.5 percent constant and only 12 million at 8 percent. Second, value falls: cap rates drift up, and the same income worth about 21.8 million at 5.5 percent is about 18.5 million at 6.5 percent. Third, floating debt costs more: two points on 10 million is 200,000 a year. Together they can turn a refinance into a 2 million cash call while value drops by over 3 million. Protection exists: fixed rates, caps, laddered maturities and lower leverage. I price each one against the stressed shortfall, not the base case, and write a one-page debt policy before the loan closes.
terms: Debt service coverage ratio (DSCR) — net operating income divided by annual loan payments.
Loan constant — the annual payment of interest and principal expressed as a percentage of the loan amount.
Interest rate cap — a hedge that pays the borrower when a floating rate rises above an agreed strike, for an upfront premium.

hostile.q: Your refinance assumes today’s rate. What if it is two points higher when you complete?
hostile.a: Then the take-out loan is about 12 million instead of 14.8, and the 2 million gap is already in the plan: it is covered by a committed equity reserve and a construction loan with two extension options. The floating portion is capped, so carry is bounded too.

title: The rules that move with the cycle
summary: Some rules that govern a development change with the cycle: central bank policy sets the price of money, bank regulators set how lenders may lend, governments add or remove measures to cool or support markets, and your own loan covenants trip when values fall. Know which rules can change during your project and build the change into the plan.
body:
Mr Shabazz, the rules that govern a development are not fixed for the life of the project. Interest rate policy, lending rules, market-cooling measures and your own loan covenants all shift with the cycle, and a plan that assumes today’s rules will hold for five years is a plan with a hidden risk.

Recall

Q. From this week, through what three channels does a rate rise reach your equity?

A. The maximum loan shrinks, the value falls as cap rates rise, and floating-rate debt costs more.

Q. From using professionals, why should instructions to an adviser be in writing?

A. So that scope, facts given and questions asked are recorded, which protects you if the advice is later disputed and stops the adviser answering a narrower question than you meant.

Q. From how law works, what is the difference between law and policy?

A. Law binds and is enforced by courts and agencies. Policy is a government’s or regulator’s chosen approach, which may or may not be written into law and can change faster.

Why this matters

REGA here. A developer reads the zoning bylaw and the building code carefully because they are visible. The rules that sink projects in a downturn are often less visible: a lending rule that stops your buyers qualifying, a new tax on a class of buyer, or a covenant in your own loan that trips when the appraised value falls. None of these are your fault. All of them are foreseeable in kind, even if not in timing.

Four layers of cycle-sensitive rules

In plain English there are four layers. First, the central bank, which sets a policy interest rate to manage inflation. Its decisions are not rules you comply with, but they set the price of almost every loan you take. Second, the bank regulator, which sets how much capital banks must hold and how they must test borrowers. When it tightens, lenders lend less even at the same interest rate. Third, government market measures: taxes or restrictions on foreign buyers, vacancy taxes, changes to transfer taxes, rent rules and incentives. Governments add these to cool hot markets and remove or add others to support weak ones. Fourth, your own contracts: loan covenants, the promises in your loan agreement that you will keep certain ratios within limits.

The professional framing is to separate what is law, what is regulation, what is policy and what is contract, because each changes differently. Contract terms change only with your counterparty’s agreement. Regulation can change by notice. Policy can change at a press conference.

Worked example one, a covenant, with hypothetical numbers. Your loan agreement contains a loan-to-value covenant: the loan may not exceed 65 percent of appraised value. The loan is $13,000,000 against a value of $21,000,000, which is about 62 percent. A downturn moves cap rates up and a new appraisal shows $18,500,000. The ratio is now $13,000,000 divided by $18,500,000, about 70 percent. You are in breach without missing a payment. A typical cure clause requires you to pay the loan down to 65 percent of the new value, which is about $12,000,000, so you owe a $1,000,000 paydown, often within a short period. Covenant definitions and cure periods are commercial terms negotiated in each loan, not standards. Read them before signing, not after the appraisal.

Say that out loud now.

Worked example two, a lending rule. You pre-sell 100 condominium units for completion in three years. Buyers qualify today for their mortgages. Before completion, rates rise and the regulator requires lenders to test borrowers at a higher rate. Hypothetically, a buyer earning $90,000 who qualified for a $400,000 mortgage now qualifies for $350,000. That buyer must find $50,000 more or fail to close. If even 15 of your 100 buyers are in that position, you have a closing problem caused by a rule that did not exist when you sold.

Two Systems

A conceptual comparison of how Canada and Guyana approach this point; verify against primary source before relying on any of it. In Canada, the Bank of Canada sets the policy rate with an inflation target, and a federal regulator of banks, the Office of the Superintendent of Financial Institutions, issues underwriting guidance for federally regulated lenders, including a qualifying test for residential mortgages [unverified — confirm independently]. Provinces and cities have added their own measures in recent years, such as taxes on certain foreign or vacant purchases, so the rule set differs by location. In Guyana, the Bank of Guyana is the central bank and supervises licensed banks [unverified — confirm independently]. The economy has grown rapidly since oil production began at the end of 2019, which brings the classic risks of a fast-moving cycle: credit expanding quickly, land prices rising ahead of incomes and policy adjusting in response. The lesson is not which system is stricter. It is that in both, the people who set lending conditions can change them during your build, and in a fast-growing economy the pace of change can be greater.

Building the change into the plan

Three habits help. Keep a short register of rules that could change during the project, with what each would do to your numbers. Negotiate covenants with headroom and with cure rights you can meet, such as the right to post cash or a letter of credit rather than repay. And for pre-sales, stress buyer qualification at a higher rate and require deposits large enough to make closing the rational choice. Professional sign-off required: a lawyer qualified in the relevant jurisdiction for any covenant, sales contract or regulatory question.

Reading a covenant clause

Four details decide whether a covenant is a safety rail or a trap. First, how value is defined: an appraisal commissioned by the lender, at the lender’s discretion, gives you no control over the timing of the test. Second, how often it is tested: an annual test is very different from a test the lender can call at any time. Third, what counts as a cure: paying down the loan in cash is the hardest; posting a letter of credit, adding collateral or depositing cash into a reserve may be easier. Fourth, the cure period: thirty days in a downturn is very short. Each of these is negotiable before signing and almost never negotiable afterwards.

A further point on government measures. When authorities cool a hot market, they rarely announce the measure years in advance, and they often apply it to transactions not yet closed. A pre-sale project that completes two years after launch may close under a different rule set from the one in force when buyers signed. Your sales contract and your lender’s pre-sale conditions should be read with that in mind, and your counsel should tell you how new measures would apply to contracts already signed.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is treating today’s lending and market rules as permanent for a multi-year project. The control is a rule-change register, reviewed at each project gate, and covenants negotiated with headroom tested in the downside case.

The beginner’s mistake

The beginner reads the interest rate and the loan amount in a term sheet and skims the covenants. The covenants are where the cycle reaches you first, often before the payments become a problem.

Callback

In Week 20 you learned that conditions and remedies decide what a contract really does when things go wrong. A loan covenant is a condition with a remedy attached, and a downturn is when it gets tested. In Week 19 you separated sources of law; today added a fourth category that moves fastest of all, which is policy.

Recap

Cycle-sensitive rules come in four layers: central bank policy, bank regulation, government market measures and your own loan covenants. Each changes differently, and any of them can change during your build. Register them, stress them and negotiate headroom.

Next: Sage, The Numbers — a full deal run through a cycle, with the exit cap rate as the variable that decides the result.
checklist: Separate every rule affecting the project into law, regulation, policy or contract.
Keep a rule-change register with the effect of each change on your numbers.
Calculate each covenant’s headroom in the downside case.
Negotiate cure rights you can actually meet, such as posting cash or a letter of credit.
Stress pre-sale buyers’ mortgage qualification at a higher rate.
Size deposits so closing is the rational choice for a buyer.
Get covenant and regulatory questions reviewed by a lawyer qualified in the jurisdiction.
head: Field checklist
speak: The rules that govern a project move with the cycle, in four layers. The central bank sets the policy rate and so the price of every loan. The bank regulator sets how lenders must test borrowers, so lending can tighten even at the same rate. Governments add or remove measures like taxes on foreign or vacant purchases. And my own loan covenants trip when values fall. On hypothetical numbers, a 13 million loan against a 21 million value is 62 percent, inside a 65 percent covenant. If a new appraisal shows 18.5 million, I am at 70 percent and in breach without missing a payment, with a 1 million paydown to cure. Pre-sales carry the same risk: a tougher qualifying test can stop buyers closing. In Canada and Guyana alike, the people who set lending conditions can change them during my build. So I keep a rule-change register, negotiate covenant headroom and stress my buyers.
terms: Loan covenant — a promise in a loan agreement to keep a ratio or condition within agreed limits, with a remedy if breached.
Cure right — a contractual right to fix a covenant breach, for example by paying down the loan or posting security, within a set period.
Macroprudential measure — a rule set by authorities to limit risk across the whole financial system, such as tighter mortgage qualification.

hostile.q: If the appraisal drops 12 percent, are you in default?
hostile.a: No. Our covenant headroom is tested at a 15 percent value fall, and if it were breached we have a 60-day right to cure by posting cash or a letter of credit, which is already sized in the reserve. The register shows that case and what we would do.

title: One deal through the cycle: the exit cap rate decides the result
summary: A hypothetical rental is built at a 7 percent yield on cost and sold after five years at three possible exit cap rates. The same building produces a profit of about 8 million, 3.8 million or 2.1 million depending only on where the cycle stands at sale. The break-even exit cap rate is the number to know before you buy land.
body:
Mr Shabazz, today we take one hypothetical building and run it to the sale, three times. Same cost, same rents, same management. Only the exit cap rate changes, and it decides whether the deal is excellent, mediocre or barely worth the risk.

Recall

Q. From this week, what is a loan-to-value covenant, and how can a downturn trip it?

A. A promise that the loan will not exceed a set share of appraised value. When cap rates rise, a new appraisal lowers value, the ratio rises above the limit, and you are in breach without missing a payment.

Q. From using professionals, what is a fee estimate worth if scope is unclear?

A. Very little. Fees follow scope, so an estimate without a defined scope and assumptions cannot be held to; ask for both before you rely on the number.

Q. From how law works, what does a court of appeal do?

A. It reviews a lower court’s decision for errors of law, and sometimes of fact, and can uphold, reverse or send it back. Its decisions bind the courts below it in common law systems.

Why this matters

Sage here. A development pro forma has hundreds of inputs, but for a building you will sell after stabilisation, one input dominates: the cap rate at which a buyer values your income on the day you sell. You do not control it. The cycle does. So the honest approach is to calculate the result at several exit cap rates and find the one at which the deal stops making money. That figure, the break-even exit cap rate, tells you how much of the cycle you can survive.

Worked example one: the base deal and three exits

All figures are hypothetical. Follow the units.

  1. Cost. Total development cost is $20,000,000, including land, hard costs, soft costs and finance costs.
  2. Stabilised income. In the first stabilised year, the building earns net operating income (NOI) of $1,400,000.
  3. Yield on cost. NOI divided by cost: $1,400,000 divided by $20,000,000 is 7.0 percent. This is what your money earns before any sale.
  4. Growth. NOI grows 2 percent a year. A buyer at the end of year 5 values the income for year 6. That is $1,400,000 times 1.02 to the power of 5, which is about $1,546,000.
  5. Value at a 5.5 percent exit cap rate. $1,546,000 divided by 0.055 is about $28,100,000.
  6. Value at 6.5 percent. $1,546,000 divided by 0.065 is about $23,800,000.
  7. Value at 7.0 percent. $1,546,000 divided by 0.070 is about $22,100,000.
  8. Profit on sale before selling costs. Value minus cost: about $8,100,000, $3,800,000 and $2,100,000 respectively.

The same building, with identical operations, produced a sale profit nearly four times larger at a 5.5 percent exit than at 7.0 percent. That spread is not a forecasting error. It is the cycle.

Say that out loud now.

Worked example two: the break-even exit cap rate

  1. Define break-even. The exit cap rate at which sale value equals total cost, so the sale itself makes no profit.
  2. Calculate. Year 6 NOI divided by cost: $1,546,000 divided by $20,000,000 is about 7.7 percent.
  3. Add selling costs. If selling costs are 2 percent of value, the buyer’s price must be about $20,400,000 for you to net $20,000,000. $1,546,000 divided by $20,400,000 is about 7.6 percent.
  4. Read it. At any exit cap rate below about 7.6 percent, the sale returns your cost. Above it, you lose money on the sale, though you may still have earned operating cash flow while you held.

Now compare with history. If, in the worst year of the last cycle, cap rates for this asset type in this market reached 7.0 percent, your break-even of 7.6 percent sits above that. The deal survives a repeat of the last downturn at the exit. If the worst year reached 8.0 percent, it does not, and you need a longer hold, lower cost or less debt.

Worked example three: the sensitivity per quarter point

  1. Value at 5.75 percent. $1,546,000 divided by 0.0575 is about $26,900,000.
  2. Change from 5.5 percent. About $1,200,000 less.
  3. Read it. Near the low end of the range, each quarter point of exit cap rate is worth roughly $1,000,000 to $1,200,000 on this building. That is more than a full year of NOI. When someone in a meeting says the exit cap rate is a judgement call, they are moving a year of income with a sentence.

Worked example four: the same three exits through your equity

  1. Capital stack. The $20,000,000 cost is funded with a $13,000,000 loan and $7,000,000 of equity.
  2. Simplification. To isolate the exit, ignore operating cash flow and selling costs, and assume the loan is repaid in full from the sale.
  3. Equity back at 5.5 percent. $28,100,000 minus $13,000,000 is $15,100,000, an equity multiple of 15.1 divided by 7, about 2.16.
  4. At 6.5 percent. $23,800,000 minus $13,000,000 is $10,800,000, a multiple of about 1.54.
  5. At 7.0 percent. $22,100,000 minus $13,000,000 is $9,100,000, a multiple of about 1.30.
Exit cap rateSale valueProfit on costEquity multiple
5.5 percent$28.1 million$8.1 million2.16
6.5 percent$23.8 million$3.8 million1.54
7.0 percent$22.1 million$2.1 million1.30

Leverage did what it always does: it widened the range. A 27 percent difference in sale value became a 66 percent difference in equity returned.

What moves the break-even

You have three levers before you commit. Lower cost: every $1,000,000 cut from cost lowers the break-even exit cap rate by roughly four tenths of a point on these numbers, which is why the land price is the most powerful lever in a late cycle. Higher income: better design or a better rent premium raises NOI. A longer hold: if the exit lands in a downturn, the ability to wait for recovery depends on debt term, not on the market. That third lever is why Rule 27 is about money, not prices.

One caution on the simplification. Leaving out operating cash flow understates every case equally, because five years of net income after interest belongs to you whichever exit you get. Leaving out selling costs flatters every case equally. Neither changes the ranking, which is why the simplified table is good for seeing the cycle, and why the full pro forma, with both included, is the one you take to a lender. Use the quick table to decide whether to keep looking at a deal, and the full model to decide whether to commit.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is setting the exit cap rate equal to today’s cap rate in a strong market, which assumes the cycle will be at the same point on the day you sell. The control: set the base exit cap rate above today’s rate, show the result at several exit rates, and compare your break-even with the worst year of the last cycle.

The beginner’s mistake

The beginner presents one exit value. The professional presents a short table: exit cap rate against sale profit and equity multiple, with the break-even marked. It takes five minutes to build and answers the first question every serious investor asks.

Callback

In Week 10 you learned the development spread: the yield on cost minus the market cap rate. Here it was 7.0 percent against a 5.5 percent market, a spread of 1.5 points. That spread is your cushion. Today showed what the cycle does to it: when the market cap rate rises toward your yield on cost, the cushion disappears. And in Week 17 you reverse engineered public deals; the same arithmetic tells you what exit cap rate a seller’s asking price assumes.

Recap

Run the sale at several exit cap rates, find the break-even, and compare it with the worst year of the last cycle. On these numbers, the same building made about 8.1 million or 2.1 million depending only on the market at sale, and each quarter point near the bottom of the range moved about a year of income.

Next: JAX, The Room — the meeting where your partner wants to buy at the top of the cycle.
checklist: Calculate year-6 NOI when the planned sale is at the end of year 5.
Show sale value at no fewer than three exit cap rates.
Compute the break-even exit cap rate, including selling costs.
Compare the break-even with the worst year of the last cycle for this asset and market.
Calculate the value of each quarter point of exit cap rate.
Set the base exit cap rate above today’s market rate.
Present the exit table, with break-even marked, in every investor pack.
head: Field checklist
speak: I ran one hypothetical rental three times. It costs 20 million and earns 1.4 million in its first stabilised year, a 7 percent yield on cost. Income grows 2 percent a year, so a buyer at the end of year 5 values about 1.546 million. At a 5.5 percent exit cap rate the building is worth about 28.1 million, a profit of about 8.1 million. At 6.5 percent it is worth 23.8 million, and at 7 percent 22.1 million, a profit of only 2.1 million. Same building, same operations. The break-even exit cap rate, where value just covers cost and 2 percent selling costs, is about 7.6 percent. If the worst year of the last cycle reached 7 percent, I survive a repeat. If it reached 8, I do not. Near the low end, each quarter point moves about a million dollars, more than a year of income.
terms: Exit cap rate — the cap rate a buyer applies to your income on the day you sell.
Break-even exit cap rate — the exit cap rate at which net sale proceeds just equal total development cost.
Forward NOI — the net operating income expected in the year after a sale, which a buyer usually values.

hostile.q: Your model exits at 5.5 percent. Where were cap rates for this asset in the last downturn?
hostile.a: Around 7 percent in the worst year, on the sales we could find. Our break-even exit cap is about 7.6 percent, so a repeat of that year still returns our cost at sale. We show the result at 5.5, 6.5 and 7.0 percent, and the base case uses 6.0, not 5.5.

title: The partner who wants to buy at the top
summary: Late in a cycle, the hardest pressure comes from your own side: a partner who wants to move fast before prices rise further. The question behind the question is fear of missing out. Answer with the break-even, the pipeline and a structure that keeps the option open without betting the company.
body:
Mr Shabazz, late in a cycle the most dangerous person in the room is often your own partner, convinced that waiting will cost more than buying. Your job is not to say no. It is to make the cycle visible on the table and offer a way to proceed that does not bet everything on timing.

Recall

Q. From this week, what is the break-even exit cap rate?

A. The exit cap rate at which net sale proceeds just equal total cost. Compare it with the worst year of the last cycle to see whether the deal survives a downturn at sale.

Q. From using professionals, what should you do if an adviser’s fee depends on the deal closing?

A. Recognise that their incentive leans toward yes, disclose it, and get an independent view on the decision itself.

Q. From how law works, can a contract override a statute?

A. Generally not where the statute is mandatory. Parties can agree terms within the room the law allows, but they cannot contract out of rules the law says apply regardless.

Why this matters

JAX here. Lenders and investors who doubt a deal are easy to read. A partner who believes in it too much is harder, because you share the goal and the excitement. At the top of a cycle, everyone you speak to has made money recently. That is the moment when the people around you are most likely to underweight risk, and when your discipline matters most.

The scene

This is a composite example. You and an equity partner are reviewing a site for a 120-unit rental. A competing buyer has appeared. The seller’s broker says the price will go up by 10 percent next week. Your partner says: “Rents are up 12 percent in two years and cap rates have never been lower. If we wait, we lose the site. Let’s waive the conditions and go firm today.” Your model shows a break-even exit cap rate of 6.4 percent, and in the last downturn cap rates in this market reached 7.0 percent.

The question behind the question

Your partner is not really asking whether the numbers work. They are asking whether you will be the person who made them miss the best deal of the year. The fear is regret, not loss. If you respond with caution as a personality trait, you lose the argument. If you respond with a number and an alternative, you change the conversation from courage to structure.

Lines to say

  • “I want this site. Here is the price at which it survives the last downturn, and here is how far today’s price is above it.”
  • “Our break-even exit cap is 6.4 percent. In the worst year of the last cycle it was 7.0. At today’s price, a repeat of that year loses money on the sale.”
  • “I counted 2,400 units approved or applied for within three kilometres. They deliver in our lease-up window.”
  • “I can go firm on a smaller first phase, or keep the conditions and offer a larger deposit. Either keeps us in the deal without betting the company on timing.”
  • “If the price goes up 10 percent next week, that is a price we will not pay. I would rather lose this site than own it at the top.”

Say that out loud now.

Lines never to say

  • “The market is going to crash.” You do not know that, and it makes you sound like you are guessing.
  • “I just have a bad feeling.” A feeling is not a reason a partner can test.
  • “Fine, let’s do it.” Agreeing to waive conditions under time pressure is exactly the decision you will review in an after-action report.
  • “You always rush things.” Make it about the deal, never the person.

When to stay silent

After you put the break-even and the downturn cap rate on the table, stop. Let your partner do the subtraction. People believe the conclusion they reach themselves far more than the one they are told. If the broker is present, do not respond to the deadline at all. A deadline set by the seller’s agent is a negotiating tactic until it is in writing from the seller.

The worked numbers behind your lines

All figures are hypothetical. Asking price for the land implies total cost of $30,000,000 and forward NOI of $1,920,000, a break-even exit cap of 6.4 percent. At a 7.0 percent exit, value is $1,920,000 divided by 0.07, about $27,400,000, a loss on sale of about $2,600,000 before selling costs. If the price rises 10 percent, land adds, say, $600,000 to cost and the break-even drops to about 6.3 percent. A smaller first phase of 60 units halves the capital at risk while keeping the option on the rest.

Holding your state

Time pressure is a physiological event as well as a commercial one. Your heart rate rises, your breathing shortens and your attention narrows to the deadline. Speak more slowly than feels natural, put your hands on the paper and refer to the numbers rather than to the argument. If you can, ask for a ten-minute break before any firm commitment and use it to read the conditions you are being asked to waive.

Time and energy on a rotating shift schedule

This month’s thread. On a rotating schedule, your judgement is not equally good at every hour. Research on shift work links sleep loss and night shifts to weaker attention and more risk-taking, though individuals differ. Practitioner habit: never sign a firm commitment, waive a condition or agree a price at the end of a night shift or after a short sleep. Schedule decisive calls in the window after your main sleep.

Put the rule in your decision journal: “No irreversible deal commitments within twelve hours after a night shift.” A partner who wants an answer at 7 in the morning after your night block can have it at 3 in the afternoon. Check with your doctor about sleep strategy for your rotation.

If your partner pushes back

Your partner may say: “The last downturn was a one-off. Things are different now.” Answer with the reference class, not with an opinion: “Maybe. Here are three downturns in this market over thirty years, and the cap rate in the worst year of each. If you think this cycle is different, which of those is the wrong reference, and why?” That moves the discussion onto evidence your partner can examine. If they still want to proceed at the higher price, ask them to write the reason in the decision journal you both keep. People are noticeably more careful about a reason they must sign.

After the meeting

Whatever you decide, record it the same day: the price offered, the break-even, the reference cap rate, the alternative you proposed and the reason for the final call. If you walk away and the price rises, you will want to know whether you were wrong or merely unlucky. If you proceed and the market turns, you will want to know whether you were careless or merely unlucky. Only a written record can tell those apart.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is letting someone else’s deadline become your decision point. The control: no firm commitment without the break-even compared with the last downturn, and no waived conditions in the same meeting the deadline was announced.

The beginner’s mistake

The beginner argues about the future: will prices rise or fall? The professional argues about the structure: what price, what phase and what conditions make the deal survive either future.

Callback

In Week 3 you studied loss aversion and the fear of missing out. A competing buyer and a broker’s deadline are designed to trigger both. In Week 6 you practised acknowledge, bridge, answer. Here: acknowledge the opportunity, bridge to the break-even, answer with a structure.

Recap

At the top of a cycle, pressure comes from inside the deal. Name the question behind the question, put the break-even and the last downturn on the table, offer a structure that keeps the option, and never waive conditions on someone else’s deadline.

Next: Kema, Quiz & Recap — six questions on cycles, a Red Pen drill and the two-minute boardroom drill.
checklist: Bring the break-even exit cap and the last downturn’s cap rate to every late-cycle meeting.
Count the approved and applied pipeline before discussing price.
Prepare a smaller-phase or keep-conditions alternative in advance.
Treat a broker’s deadline as a tactic until it is in writing from the seller.
Ask for a break before any firm commitment.
Never waive conditions in the meeting where a deadline is announced.
No irreversible commitments within twelve hours after a night shift.
head: Field checklist
speak: Late in a cycle, the hardest pressure comes from my own partner. A competing buyer appears, the broker says the price rises next week, and my partner wants to waive conditions today. The question behind the question is fear of regret. So I answer with numbers and a structure. I say: our break-even exit cap is 6.4 percent, and in the worst year of the last cycle it was 7.0, so at today’s price a repeat loses about 2.6 million on sale. I name the pipeline delivering into our lease-up. Then I offer a way to stay in: a smaller first phase, or a bigger deposit with the conditions kept. I never say the market will crash, and I never agree under a broker’s deadline. After I put the numbers down, I stay silent and let my partner do the subtraction. And I never make an irreversible commitment straight after a night shift.
terms: Fear of missing out — the anxiety that others are profiting from an opportunity you are passing up, which pushes people toward rushed decisions.
Firm commitment — the point at which a purchase agreement’s conditions are waived and the deposit is at risk.
Phasing — dividing a project into stages so that later stages can be delayed, resized or abandoned.

hostile.q: If we lose this site because you wanted conditions, who explains that to our investors?
hostile.a: I will, with the numbers. At this price a repeat of the last downturn loses money on sale. I have offered a larger deposit with conditions kept, and a firm first phase. If the seller rejects both, we have lost a site at the top of the market, which is a loss our investors can survive.

role: Chief of staff and learning coach
title: Cycles week: quiz, recap and the Red Pen
summary: Six questions test the supply lag, cap rates and rates, Rule 27, the three channels of a rate rise, covenants and the break-even exit cap rate. The Red Pen drill finds the planted defects in a late-cycle investment memo, and the boardroom drill explains cycles in two minutes.
body:
Mr Shabazz, this week showed that cycles are not weather to complain about but arithmetic to plan for: supply arrives late, credit moves fast, cap rates follow rates, and the exit cap rate decides the result. Today you test it, then you mark up a memo that forgot all of it.

Recall

Q. From this week, what should you do when a broker announces a price rise next week?

A. Treat it as a tactic until it is in writing from the seller, and never waive conditions in the same meeting.

Q. From using professionals, why does an adviser’s incentive matter?

A. Because advice tends to lean toward the outcome that pays the adviser. Disclose the incentive and get an independent view where it matters.

Q. From how law works, what is the role of the courts in interpreting a statute?

A. To decide what its words mean when applied to real facts, which can extend or narrow its practical effect.

The six questions

Question 1. Why do property markets overshoot? Answer: Because of the supply lag. Developers react to the same strong rents at the same time, and their buildings deliver years later, together, often into a weaker market.

Question 2. A building earns $1,000,000 of net operating income. What is it worth at a 5 percent and a 6 percent cap rate? Answer: $20,000,000 and about $16,700,000, a fall of about 17 percent from a one-point move.

Question 3. What was the root cause of Olympia & York’s failure, and what is Rule 27? Answer: A maturity mismatch on a concentrated bet: a giant single-market project at the top of a cycle, funded partly with short money. Rule 27: fund long projects with long money, never let a refinancing date fall where a downturn can reach it unprotected, and never let one project grow larger than the balance sheet can carry through the worst year of the last cycle.

Question 4. Through what three channels does a rate rise reach your equity? Answer: The loan the income supports shrinks, value falls as cap rates rise, and floating-rate debt costs more.

Question 5. How can you be in breach of a loan without missing a payment? Answer: Through a covenant, such as a loan-to-value limit, that trips when a new appraisal shows a lower value.

Question 6. What is the break-even exit cap rate, and what do you compare it with? Answer: The exit cap rate at which net sale proceeds equal total cost. Compare it with the cap rate in the worst year of the last cycle.

Recap

Four clocks run at different speeds: demand, supply, credit and pricing. Read your position rather than predict the turn. A rate rise reaches you three ways at once, rules and covenants move with the cycle, and the exit cap rate dominates the result. Size your debt, your bets and your exit assumptions so the worst year of the last cycle is survivable.

Say that out loud now.

Red Pen

Read this hypothetical extract from an investment memo and find the defects before reading the list.

Investment memo, hypothetical. Market: rents have grown 12 percent in two years and supply is limited. Exit: we assume a sale in year 5 at a 4.75 percent cap rate, in line with current market pricing. Debt: a $15,000,000 floating-rate construction loan, with a refinance in year 3 at current rates. Conclusion: the project produces a strong return under all reasonable scenarios.

The defects:

  1. “Supply is limited” is an adjective, not a count. No pipeline of approved and applied projects, no delivery dates.
  2. Past rent growth projected as normal. Twelve percent in two years is the signal every competitor is reading, not a base case.
  3. Exit cap rate equal to today’s. The memo assumes the cycle is at the same point on the day of sale. The base exit should be above current pricing.
  4. No break-even exit cap rate and no comparison with the last downturn.
  5. Floating debt with no hedge. No cap, no cost per point of rate rise.
  6. Refinance “at current rates.” The take-out loan is not sized in a higher-rate case, so the refinance shortfall is unknown.
  7. “Under all reasonable scenarios” with no scenarios shown. Show the table or delete the sentence.

Boardroom drill

Explain this week to a board in two minutes. Set a timer, speak, then compare with the model answer.

Model answer: “Property moves in waves because buildings take years to deliver while demand and credit change in months, so developers who react to the same strong rents deliver together into a softer market. Value is income divided by the cap rate, and cap rates follow interest rates loosely and with a lag; a one-point move can take a sixth off value and nearly half off our equity. A rate rise reaches us three ways at once: a smaller take-out loan, a lower value and more expensive floating debt. Rules move with the cycle too: lending tests tighten and our own covenants trip when appraisals fall. So we do not try to time the top. We count the pipeline, set our exit cap rate above today’s, know our break-even exit cap rate and compare it with the worst year of the last cycle. We fund long projects with long money, keep refinancing dates out of a downturn’s reach and never let one project outgrow the balance sheet.”

One exercise for this week

Pick any market you know, with no project attached. Find, from public sources, the approximate cap rate for one asset type in the strongest and weakest years you can identify over the last fifteen years, and the long government bond yield in each of those years. Write down the spread in each. You now have a rough map of how far pricing has moved in that market, and a reference figure for every break-even exit cap rate you calculate there.

How to score your boardroom drill

Listen to your recording and check five things. Did you open with the bottom line, that cycles are planned for rather than predicted? Did you state one number aloud, such as a one-point cap rate move taking about 17 percent off value? Did you name the three channels of a rate rise without notes? Did you mention the exit cap rate and the break-even, and what you compare it with? And did you finish with the rule, not with a forecast? Score one point for each. Four or five means you own the week. Three or fewer means replay Day 3 and Day 5 before moving on.

Listen also for one weakness that most people show the first time: saying what the market will do. Any sentence that begins “I think rates will” or “prices are going to” is a prediction, and this week was about not needing one. Replace it with what you would do if you are wrong.

A final check on composure. If your answer sped up when you reached the numbers, slow the numbers down on the second attempt and leave a short pause after each one. A number spoken with a pause sounds certain; the same number rushed sounds like a guess.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk this week is believing that because the cycle cannot be predicted, it can be ignored. It cannot be predicted, which is exactly why it must be designed for.

The beginner’s mistake

The beginner asks whether now is a good time to build. The professional asks what has to be true at the exit for the deal to work, and how often that has been true before.

Callback

In Week 2 you learned the pre-mortem: imagine the project has failed and ask why. Run one on any late-cycle deal and the first answer is almost always the same: we sold into a weaker market than we assumed, and the debt came due before it recovered. This week gave you the numbers to test that answer before it happens.

terms: Late-cycle signal — evidence that a market is near its peak, such as loosening lender terms, a swelling pipeline and thin cap rate spreads.
Refinance shortfall — the cash needed when the new loan available at maturity is smaller than the loan it must repay.
Downturn reference case — a scenario built from the actual conditions of the worst year of the last full cycle.

hostile.q: Everyone is buying in this market. Why should we be the ones who wait?
hostile.a: We are not waiting; we are pricing. At a price where the break-even exit cap rate sits above the worst year of the last cycle, we buy today. Above that price we are betting on timing, and we do not fund timing bets with borrowed money.
